system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2164-08-06 09:44:00 to 2164-08-07 16:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of Addison’s disease and hypothyroidism, was admitted after a motor vehicle accident two days prior, during which she briefly lost consciousness and sustained a minor wrist burn. She developed a persistent bifrontal headache with photophobia, phonophobia, and vomiting, preventing her from taking her home steroid and thyroid medications. She was treated with IV fluids, IV hydrocortisone for adrenal coverage, and IV pain and anti-nausea medications. Her symptoms improved rapidly, and she was restarted on oral prednisone, Florinef, and Synthroid. Neurologic exams and repeat imaging were normal, supporting a diagnosis of migraine and post-concussion headache. She tolerated a regular diet, ambulated without issue, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to resume her baseline medications and monitor for worsening symptoms.
problems: Migraine without aura, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Other motor vehicle traffic accident involving collision with motor vehicle injuring driver of motor vehicle other than motorcycle

Brief Hospital Course:
*)Nausea/vomiting, malaise - in the setting of her history of 
Addison's disease and her electrolyte abnormalities, as well as 
symptoms similar to her prior presentations, she was admitted 
for management of likely adrenal crisis. Her blood pressure 
remained stable throughout her hospitalization. She was 
afebrile, and there was no evidence of infection as a 
precipitating event. After treatment with high-dose IV steroids, 
she felt much better and on the day of discharge her labs had 
markedly improved and she was able to eat and ambulate without 
difficulty. She was discharged on a rapid steroid taper, after a 
brief informal consultation of the Endocrinology fellow. She 
will have repeat labs drawn at her primary care doctor's office

her endocrinologist. A message has been left with her primary 
care doctor to follow up her labs. 
.
*)Acute renal failure - on admission had an elevation of her 
creatinine to 1.8, which was thought to be pre-renal in etiology 
in the setting of her recent nausea/vomiting and decreased po 
intake. Her creatinine improved after IV fluids and was 1.2 on 
the day of discharge. She was to follow up with her 
endocrinologist, with repeat labs to be performed at that time.
.
*)Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo - on the day of admission 
experienced vertigo upon turning her head. Had had similar 
symptoms the prior year, but had not been evaluated due to other 
issues surrounding her recent surgery at that time. Symptoms at 
that time resolved spontaneously. She did not have any 
neurologic deficits on exam or history. ___ did not 
produce the classic nystagmus, but did seem to improve her 
symptoms. She was given instructions regarding Epley maneuvers, 
as well as precautions for calling her doctor or returning to 
the ED for any neurologic symptoms or persistent vertigo. On the 
day of discharge her symptoms had resolved and she was able to 
ambulate and perform other activities (i.e. knitting) without 
difficulty.
.
*)Hypertension - metoprolol was held during her hospitalization. 
While her blood pressures remained in the normal range, they 
were at the lower end of that range. She is to follow up at her 
primary care doctor's office in a few days for repeat labs; 
metoprolol may be re-started at that time, or on her visit with 
her endocrinologist. 
.
*)Hypothyroidism - her home dose of levothyroxine was continued.
.
*)Depression/anxiety - her home medications were continued.
.

diagnoses.long_title: Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel. I’ve been reviewing your case. You came in yesterday with nausea, vomiting, and fatigue—can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started Friday night. I’ve had two episodes of vomiting each day. I didn’t come in sooner because I had guests over the weekend and thought it might pass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you’ve had similar episodes before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about every two months for the past year. It feels like my Addison’s disease acting up—fatigue, nausea, craving salty things like saltines. I get a heavy headache too, which I think is from high potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your labs when you came in showed low sodium and high potassium, which fits with an adrenal crisis. We gave you IV hydrocortisone in the ER to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh good. I was worried I hadn’t taken enough steroids. But I did keep taking my usual prednisone and Florinef.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing. But during times of stress or illness, your body needs more. That’s why we gave you a higher dose IV to cover the crisis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. I’m feeling a bit better now—less nauseous and actually hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We also gave you IV fluids to help with dehydration. Your blood pressure has been stable, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did notice I felt a little dizzy when I turned my head this morning. It was like the room spun.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned vertigo. We think it might be benign positional vertigo—something that can happen on its own or after illness. It’s not related to your brain, just the inner ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I had something like that last year, but it went away. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious at all. We didn’t see the typical eye movements, but we can show you a simple maneuver—Epley maneuver—that often helps. You can do it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be great. I’d like to avoid this spinning feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse demonstrate it later. Now, your kidney function was a bit off when you came in—creatinine was elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the vomiting? I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We think it’s pre-renal—meaning your kidneys are getting less blood flow due to dehydration. After fluids, your creatinine improved to 1.2, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about my kidneys. I’ve had Addison’s for years, so I try to stay on top of things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very aware of your body, which helps. We’ve continued your levothyroxine for your hypothyroidism, and your mood meds—Celexa and clonazepam—are still being given as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take those every day. I’ve been feeling okay emotionally—just tired from being sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’re not seeing signs of infection, so we think this was just a flare of your Addison’s due to stress on your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just did a quick respiratory check—everything looks good. Your oxygen levels are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been breathing fine. No chest pain or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to update you—your repeat labs look much better. Sodium is up to 134, potassium is 4.7, and creatinine is now 1.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I’m out of the woods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re confident this adrenal episode is resolving. We’ll start you on a short course of oral hydrocortisone to taper down over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not my usual prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your usual prednisone after the taper. Hydrocortisone is closer to your body’s natural cortisol and better for stress dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what about my blood pressure? I usually take metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it because your pressures have been on the lower side—around 106/60. You can restart it after discharge, probably at your primary care visit in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse showed me the Epley maneuver. It felt a little strange, but the dizziness didn’t come back after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. It often works quickly. If it comes back, you can repeat it at home or let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning! You’re looking well. We’re planning to discharge you today if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, finish the hydrocortisone taper exactly as written—50mg every 8 hours for two doses, then down to 25mg every 8 hours, then every 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then back to my 5mg prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume your regular prednisone and Florinef as before. Also, take your levothyroxine in the morning on an empty stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. Check with your primary care doctor in a few days—they’ll decide when to restart it based on your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Celexa? I saw it’s now 20mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we increased it to 20mg daily. You were on 10mg, but given your history of anxiety and depression, your care team felt this was appropriate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take half a tablet. I hope it helps with the stress of these flare-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also arranged for you to get labs done at your doctor’s office two days after discharge. Please follow up with your endocrinologist soon after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Should I call if I feel sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—any nausea, vomiting, fatigue, or trouble keeping meds down, call your doctor right away. And if dizziness returns or you have any new neurologic symptoms, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re just drawing a little blood for your final labs. This is routine before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No problem. I’m glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable, and you’ve been walking and eating well. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: finish the steroid taper, follow up on labs, and take care of yourself. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon!

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with a history of Addison’s disease, hypothyroidism, and hypertension, was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and fatigue over three days, consistent with an adrenal crisis. She had typical symptoms including salt cravings and headache, and labs showed hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. She received IV hydrocortisone and fluids in the emergency department and was admitted for monitoring. Her condition improved rapidly, with normalization of electrolytes and kidney function. She also experienced benign paroxysmal positional vertigo on admission, which resolved with Epley maneuvers. She was discharged on a rapid hydrocortisone taper, with instructions to resume her baseline prednisone and Florinef, hold metoprolol pending follow-up, and increase Celexa to 20mg daily. She was advised to follow up with her primary care provider for labs and with her endocrinologist, and to seek care if symptoms recurred.
